subject: chemistry

items.q: Dilute hydrochloric acid is added to a piece of magnesium ribbon. What are the products?
items.correct: Magnesium chloride and hydrogen gas
items.misconception: Magnesium chloride and water
items.why: Salt and water is the first product pair students meet and it is repeated so often that it becomes the answer to any acid question. Sort the reactions by what the acid meets: metal gives hydrogen, base or alkali gives water, carbonate gives water and carbon dioxide.
items.random_wrong: Magnesium chlorate plus hydrogen

items.q: Pieces of magnesium, zinc, iron and copper are each added to dilute sulfuric acid. Only the copper gives no bubbles. Why?
items.correct: Copper is too unreactive to release hydrogen
items.misconception: Copper does react, but far too slowly to spot
items.why: The rule is first met as 'acid + metal → salt + hydrogen', which reads like a rule for all metals, and the metals handed out in class are chosen because they react. The specification says acids react with some metals. A metal only releases hydrogen if it is more reactive than hydrogen; copper, silver and gold are not.
items.random_wrong: Copper makes a salt and water but no gas

items.q: Which equation correctly represents the reaction of zinc with dilute sulfuric acid?
items.correct: Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂
items.misconception: Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂O
items.why: Salt and water is the first product pair students meet and it is repeated so often that it becomes the answer to any acid question. Sort the reactions by what the acid meets: metal gives hydrogen, base or alkali gives water, carbonate gives water and carbon dioxide.
items.random_wrong: Zn + 2H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + 2H₂

items.q: Iron filings are warmed with dilute hydrochloric acid. Which salt is formed?
items.correct: Iron(II) chloride, FeCl₂
items.misconception: Iron(III) chloride, FeCl₃
items.why: Iron(III) compounds are met first in rusting, and the 3+ ion is the one students remember. Dilute acid takes iron only as far as Fe²⁺, so the salt is iron(II) chloride and two chloride ions balance the charge.
items.random_wrong: Iron(II) chlorate, Fe(ClO₃)₂

items.q: (HT) Why is the reaction between zinc and dilute hydrochloric acid described as a redox reaction?
items.correct: Zinc atoms lose electrons and hydrogen ions gain them
items.misconception: Zinc gains electrons and hydrogen ions lose them
items.why: OIL RIG is memorised as a phrase but not attached to a picture, so the two halves get swapped under pressure. Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain — of electrons. A metal atom becoming a positive ion must have lost electrons.
items.random_wrong: No oxygen is involved, so it is not a redox change

items.q: (HT) In the reaction Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂, which species is oxidised?
items.correct: Magnesium, as it loses two electrons
items.misconception: Hydrogen ions, as they lose electrons
items.why: 'Reduced' is heard as 'used up' or 'made smaller', and it is the metal that visibly disappears. Reduction means gain of electrons. The metal loses electrons, so it is the hydrogen ions that are reduced.
items.random_wrong: Chloride ions, as they change place

items.q: (HT) Which line shows the reduction step when iron reacts with dilute sulfuric acid, and names it correctly?
items.correct: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂, a gain of electrons
items.misconception: Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻, the loss of electrons
items.why: 'Reduced' is heard as 'used up' or 'made smaller', and it is the metal that visibly disappears. Reduction means gain of electrons. The metal loses electrons, so it is the hydrogen ions that are reduced.
items.random_wrong: H₂ → 2H⁺ + 2e⁻, written in reverse

items.q: Copper(II) oxide is added to warm dilute sulfuric acid. What is produced?
items.correct: Copper sulfate and water only
items.misconception: Copper sulfate, water and hydrogen
items.why: The acid-metal reaction is done first and is the most visually striking, so hydrogen becomes the expected gas. The hydrogen ions from the acid end up in water when the acid meets a base or alkali. Hydrogen gas needs a metal to give up electrons.
items.random_wrong: Copper sulfate and carbon dioxide

items.q: Calcium carbonate chips are dropped into dilute nitric acid and the mixture fizzes. What are the three products?
items.correct: Calcium nitrate, water and carbon dioxide
items.misconception: Calcium nitrate and water, no gas
items.why: Students learn 'acid + base → salt + water' as the neutralisation equation and apply it to carbonates too. A carbonate also supplies carbon and oxygen, so carbon dioxide is released as well; that is the fizzing that is seen.
items.random_wrong: Calcium nitrate, water and hydrogen

items.q: Which substance is correctly described as an alkali?
items.correct: Sodium hydroxide, a soluble metal hydroxide
items.misconception: Copper(II) oxide, which is an insoluble base
items.why: The two words are used side by side in lessons and both are 'the opposite of acid', so they are treated as synonyms. An alkali is a soluble base. If it does not dissolve to give a solution containing OH⁻ ions, it is a base only.
items.random_wrong: Copper hydroxide, which will not dissolve

items.q: Which statement about the salts made by acids is correct?
items.correct: Nitric acid produces nitrates
items.misconception: Sulfuric acid produces sulfides
items.why: Sulfide is the shorter, more familiar word, and the oxygen in the sulfate ion is easy to forget. Sulfide is S²⁻, made from sulfur alone. Sulfuric acid, H₂SO₄, supplies the sulfate ion SO₄²⁻.
items.random_wrong: Hydrochloric acid gives chlorates

items.q: Which pair of reactants would produce the salt potassium sulfate, K₂SO₄?
items.correct: Sulfuric acid and potassium hydroxide
items.misconception: Hydrochloric acid and potassium hydroxide
items.why: The metal is written first in the salt's name, so it seems to be the part that matters. Both halves matter. The acid decides the second half of the name and the negative ion in the formula.
items.random_wrong: Nitric acid and potassium hydroxide solution

items.q: In a reaction between an acid and a base, where does the positive ion in the salt come from?
items.correct: From the base, alkali or carbonate used
items.misconception: From the acid that is being used
items.why: The acid is the substance being 'used' in the reaction, so it is assumed to be the source of everything in the product. Split the salt in two: the positive ion comes from the base, alkali or carbonate, and the negative ion comes from the acid.
items.random_wrong: From the water formed in the reaction

items.q: Predict the products of the reaction between dilute hydrochloric acid and zinc oxide.
items.correct: Zinc chloride and water only
items.misconception: Zinc chloride and hydrogen gas
items.why: The acid-metal reaction is done first and is the most visually striking, so hydrogen becomes the expected gas. The hydrogen ions from the acid end up in water when the acid meets a base or alkali. Hydrogen gas needs a metal to give up electrons.
items.random_wrong: Zinc chlorate plus water

items.q: Calcium ions are Ca²⁺ and nitrate ions are NO₃⁻. What is the formula of calcium nitrate?
items.correct: Ca(NO₃)₂
items.misconception: CaNO₃
items.why: Formulae are copied as symbol pairs without checking that the positive and negative charges cancel. Count the charge. 2+ must be cancelled by two 1− ions, so two nitrates are needed and brackets show that.
items.random_wrong: Ca₂(NO₃)₂

items.q: Zinc ions are Zn²⁺ and sulfate ions are SO₄²⁻. What is the formula of zinc sulfate?
items.correct: ZnSO₄
items.misconception: Zn₂SO₄
items.why: Formulae are copied as symbol pairs without checking that the positive and negative charges cancel. Count the charge. 2+ must be cancelled by two 1− ions, so two nitrates are needed and brackets show that.
items.random_wrong: Zn(SO₄)₂

items.q: When making a soluble salt, why is the insoluble solid added to the acid until no more reacts?
items.correct: To be sure that all of the acid has been used up
items.misconception: To make the reaction happen much more quickly
items.why: More reactant usually means a faster reaction, so that is the reason that comes to mind. The purpose is completeness, not rate: leftover solid proves that no acid remains to contaminate the salt.
items.random_wrong: To leave some spare acid to help crystals form

items.q: Which solid should be added to dilute sulfuric acid to prepare copper sulfate by this method?
items.correct: Copper(II) oxide powder
items.misconception: Copper metal turnings
items.why: The rule is first met as 'acid + metal → salt + hydrogen', which reads like a rule for all metals, and the metals handed out in class are chosen because they react. The specification says acids react with some metals. A metal only releases hydrogen if it is more reactive than hydrogen; copper, silver and gold are not.
items.random_wrong: Sodium hydroxide solution

items.q: After the excess solid has been filtered off, where is the salt?
items.correct: Dissolved in the filtrate that passes through
items.misconception: Trapped in the residue left on the filter paper
items.why: Filtering is usually met as a way of collecting a solid product, so the solid left behind is assumed to be what you want. The salt made here is soluble, so it is in solution. The residue is the unreacted solid you are throwing away.
items.random_wrong: Split evenly between the residue and the filtrate

items.q: Which sequence produces a pure, dry sample of a soluble salt from an insoluble base?
items.correct: Add excess solid, filter, then crystallise
items.misconception: Add excess acid, filter it, then crystallise
items.why: The acid is seen as the active ingredient, so having more of it feels safer. Excess acid cannot be filtered off and would stay in the crystals. Excess solid can be filtered out, so the solid is the one to have spare.
items.random_wrong: Filter the acid first, then add the solid oxide

items.q: How is a solution of a salt best turned into good crystals of the solid salt?
items.correct: Evaporate some water, then leave it to crystallise
items.misconception: Boil the solution dry over a roaring flame
items.why: Evaporating to dryness looks like the fastest route to a solid, and the crystallising step seems like waiting for nothing. Strong heating gives a powder and can decompose the salt or drive off water of crystallisation. Concentrate the solution, then leave it to crystallise.
items.random_wrong: Add more water until crystals begin to appear

items.q: In Required practical 1, how is the salt solution evaporated once the excess solid has been filtered off?
items.correct: Using a water bath or an electric heater
items.misconception: With a roaring Bunsen flame under the dish
items.why: One heat source is expected for the whole experiment, and the Bunsen is the familiar one. The specification names a water bath or electric heater for the evaporation, because gentle heating protects the crystals.
items.random_wrong: By filtering the solution through paper

items.q: Which ion do all acids produce in aqueous solution?
items.correct: Hydrogen ions, H⁺
items.misconception: Hydroxide ions, OH⁻
items.why: The two ions are learned as a pair and are easily swapped; the charge on H⁺ is also often written the wrong way. Acids produce H⁺, a positive ion. Alkalis produce OH⁻. The acid's own H⁺ is what makes the solution acidic.
items.random_wrong: Chloride ions, Cl⁻

items.q: What do aqueous solutions of alkalis contain?
items.correct: Hydroxide ions, OH⁻
items.misconception: The hydrogen ions, H⁺
items.why: Sodium hydroxide contains an H in its formula, so hydrogen ions seem to be present. The H in OH⁻ is bonded to the oxygen within the hydroxide ion; it is not released as H⁺.
items.random_wrong: Hydrogen molecules, H₂

items.q: Which statement about the pH scale is correct?
items.correct: It runs from 0 to 14 and measures acidity or alkalinity
items.misconception: It runs from 1 to 14 and measures the acid strength
items.why: Classroom charts often start at 1, and 'strong acid' and 'low pH' are used loosely as if they meant the same thing. The scale is 0 to 14. pH measures acidity, which depends on hydrogen ion concentration and so on both strength and concentration.
items.random_wrong: It runs from 0 to 7 for acids and no further

items.q: Four solutions have pH values of 2, 7, 9 and 13. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: The solution at pH 2 is acidic and pH 13 is alkaline
items.misconception: The solution at pH 2 must be alkaline and pH 13 acidic
items.why: A small number is read as 'a small amount of acid', so the direction of the scale is inverted. The scale runs the other way: the lower the pH, the greater the hydrogen ion concentration and the more acidic the solution.
items.random_wrong: The solution at pH 7 does not contain any ions

items.q: Which equation represents the neutralisation of an acid by an alkali?
items.correct: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O
items.misconception: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O₂
items.why: The equation is recalled as a shape rather than counted, and H₂O₂ looks like a plausible product of two ions. One H⁺ and one OH⁻ contain two H, one O in total, which is exactly H₂O. Any coefficient must appear on both sides.
items.random_wrong: 2H⁺ + 2OH⁻ → H₂O

items.q: A few drops of universal indicator are added to a solution and the colour is matched to a chart. What does this give?
items.correct: An approximate value for the solution's pH
items.misconception: An exact pH value, correct to two decimal places
items.why: The chart shows numbered colours, so it looks like a precise scale. Universal indicator is a wide range indicator: it gives an approximate pH. A pH probe is needed for a precise value.
items.random_wrong: The concentration of the acid in mol per dm³

items.q: What is measured in a titration between an acid and an alkali?
items.correct: The volumes of the solutions that react together
items.misconception: The mass of salt made when they are mixed
items.why: The salt preparation practical is done first, where a solid product is collected and weighed. Titration is a volume measurement. No product is isolated during it.
items.random_wrong: The temperature rise during the reaction

items.q: In a titration, how should the 25.0 cm³ of alkali be measured into the conical flask?
items.correct: With a pipette and a safety filler
items.misconception: With a measuring cylinder poured in
items.why: All three pieces of glassware measure volume, so they feel interchangeable. A pipette delivers a fixed volume accurately; a measuring cylinder is far less precise. The burette is for the solution added gradually.
items.random_wrong: From the burette holding the acid

items.q: Why is a single indicator such as phenolphthalein used in a titration rather than universal indicator?
items.correct: It changes colour sharply at the end point
items.misconception: It shows the pH at every stage of the titration
items.why: Showing more information seems better, and the pH is what the reaction is changing. A titration needs one sharp change at the end point. A single indicator such as phenolphthalein gives that; a gradual colour range does not.
items.random_wrong: Universal indicator reacts with the acid used

items.q: In Required practical 2, a student records titres of 24.10, 23.55 and 23.60 cm³. What should be done next?
items.correct: Average the two concordant titres only
items.misconception: Take the mean of all three titres recorded
items.why: Averaging everything is the general rule taught for repeat readings, and discarding data feels like cheating. The first titre is a rough one. Concordant titres agree within 0.10 cm³, and only those are averaged.
items.random_wrong: Use the largest titre, because it is safest

items.q: (HT) How many moles are there in 20.0 cm³ of hydrochloric acid of concentration 0.100 mol/dm³?
items.misconception: 2.00 mol
items.why: The unit conversion is a separate step that is easy to skip, and once it is remembered it is sometimes applied again. 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³. Convert once, at the start, and check that the answer is a sensible size.

items.q: (HT) 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide is neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid, reacting 1:1. What is the concentration of the alkali?
items.correct: 0.0800 mol/dm³
items.misconception: 0.00800 mol/dm³
items.why: The unit conversion is a separate step that is easy to skip, and once it is remembered it is sometimes applied again. 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³. Convert once, at the start, and check that the answer is a sensible size.
items.random_wrong: 0.125 mol/dm³

items.q: (HT) A sodium hydroxide solution has a concentration of 0.0800 mol/dm³. What is this in g/dm³? (Mᵣ of NaOH = 40)
items.correct: 3.2 g/dm³
items.misconception: 0.002 g/dm³
items.why: Moles and mass are linked by both multiplying and dividing in different problems, so the direction is guessed. Mass = moles × Mᵣ, so concentration in g/dm³ = concentration in mol/dm³ × Mᵣ.
items.random_wrong: 0.08 g/dm³

items.q: (HT) What does it mean to say that hydrochloric acid is a strong acid?
items.correct: It is completely ionised in aqueous solution
items.misconception: It contains a large amount of acid in each dm³
items.why: In everyday speech a 'strong' drink is a concentrated one, and both words describe something powerful. Keep the two ideas apart: concentration is how much acid is there; strength is what fraction of it has ionised.
items.random_wrong: It is no more ionised than a weak acid is

items.q: (HT) Which set contains only weak acids?
items.correct: Ethanoic acid, citric acid and carbonic acid
items.misconception: Hydrochloric, nitric and sulfuric acids
items.why: Ionisation is presented as what acids do, and partial ionisation is a harder idea to picture. In a weak acid only a small fraction of the molecules release their H⁺ at any time, so the hydrogen ion concentration is lower.
items.random_wrong: Ethanoic acid, nitric and sulfuric acids

items.q: (HT) A bottle is labelled 'concentrated ethanoic acid'. What does the word concentrated tell you?
items.correct: A large amount of acid is dissolved in each dm³
items.misconception: The ethanoic acid in it is completely ionised
items.why: In everyday speech a 'strong' drink is a concentrated one, and both words describe something powerful. Keep the two ideas apart: concentration is how much acid is there; strength is what fraction of it has ionised.
items.random_wrong: There is only a little acid dissolved in each dm³

items.q: (HT) The pH of a solution falls from 5 to 3. How does the hydrogen ion concentration change?
items.correct: It increases by a factor of 100
items.misconception: It increases by a factor of 2
items.why: The pH difference is treated as a multiplier on a linear scale. Each pH unit is a factor of 10, so two units is 10 × 10 = 100.
items.random_wrong: It increases by a factor of 1000

items.q: (HT) Equal concentrations of hydrochloric acid and ethanoic acid are compared. Which has the lower pH, and why?
items.correct: Hydrochloric acid, as it fully ionises
items.misconception: Ethanoic acid, as it ionises only partly
items.why: Strength and pH are linked in the right way but the direction of the pH scale is inverted. More hydrogen ions means a lower pH. The stronger acid ionises more, so its pH is lower.
items.random_wrong: Hydrochloric acid, as it is more concentrated

items.q: (HT) Solution X has pH 4 and solution Y has pH 7. What can be said about their hydrogen ion concentrations?
items.correct: X has 1000 times the hydrogen ion concentration of Y
items.misconception: X has just 3 times the hydrogen ion concentration of Y
items.why: The pH difference is treated as a multiplier on a linear scale. Each pH unit is a factor of 10, so two units is 10 × 10 = 100.
items.random_wrong: Y has the higher hydrogen ion concentration here

items.q: Does carbon dioxide form when an acid reacts with a metal or a metal oxide?
items.correct: No. Carbon dioxide is only produced when the acid reacts with a carbonate.
items.misconception: Acid reactions fizz, and fizzing means carbon dioxide, so carbon dioxide is always a product.
items.why: The carbonate reaction is memorable because of the vigorous fizzing, and the gas from an acid-metal reaction also looks like bubbles. Carbon must come from somewhere. Only a carbonate contains carbon, so only a carbonate can give carbon dioxide.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which salt does hydrochloric acid produce?
items.correct: Chlorides, containing the Cl⁻ ion.
items.misconception: Hydrochloric acid produces chlorates.
items.why: Chlorate sounds like a tidy '-ate' ending to match nitrate and sulfate, so students regularise the name. Chlorate, ClO₃⁻, contains oxygen and is not made by hydrochloric acid. Hydrochloric acid gives chlorides.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Balance: Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂
items.correct: It is already balanced as written.
items.misconception: Extra numbers must be added, for example doubling the acid or writing the hydrogen as 2H.
items.why: Students balance by changing whatever is nearest rather than counting atoms of every element on both sides. Count each element: 1 Zn, 2 H, 1 S and 4 O on both sides. Hydrogen gas is always H₂, never a lone H.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂ a redox reaction, given that no oxygen is involved?
items.correct: Yes. Electrons are transferred from magnesium to hydrogen ions.
items.misconception: Without oxygen there can be no oxidation, so it is not redox.
items.why: Oxidation is introduced as gain of oxygen, and that first definition sticks. At Higher tier redox is defined by electron transfer. Gain and loss of oxygen is only one example of it.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which salt does nitric acid produce?
items.correct: Nitrates, containing the NO₃⁻ ion.
items.misconception: Nitric acid produces nitrides, or else nitrites.
items.why: The three names sound almost identical and the endings are not connected to the actual ions. Nitride is N³⁻ and nitrite is NO₂⁻. Nitric acid, HNO₃, supplies the nitrate ion NO₃⁻.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is Zn₂(SO₄)₂ an acceptable formula for zinc sulfate?
items.correct: No. The ratio simplifies to ZnSO₄.
items.misconception: Any ratio that balances the charges will do, so it need not be simplified.
items.why: Students cross over the charges mechanically and never check whether the subscripts share a common factor. A formula uses the simplest whole-number ratio of ions, so Zn₂(SO₄)₂ must be reduced to ZnSO₄.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can sodium hydroxide solution be used as the excess substance in this preparation?
items.correct: No. The method needs an insoluble solid that can be filtered off.
items.misconception: Any base will do, including a solution of an alkali.
items.why: Both are bases and both neutralise the acid, so the difference in solubility is overlooked. Excess alkali would stay dissolved and contaminate the salt. An insoluble oxide, hydroxide or carbonate can be filtered out.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How should the crystals be dried?
items.correct: Pat them between filter papers, or leave them in a warm place.
items.misconception: Rinse them with more acid, or heat them strongly, to clean and dry them.
items.why: Washing is associated with purifying, and the acid is the liquid to hand. Acid would contaminate the sample and strong heating decomposes it. Drying is done gently, without adding anything.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which gives a more precise pH: universal indicator or a pH probe?
items.correct: A pH probe. Universal indicator gives only an approximate value.
items.misconception: The indicator is more reliable because you can see the colour for yourself.
items.why: Colour is direct evidence, and the probe is a black box that has to be trusted. Matching a colour to a chart gives a value to the nearest unit at best; a calibrated probe gives a numerical reading.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Two solutions have pH 7 and pH 9. What does that tell you?
items.correct: The first is neutral; the second is alkaline.
items.misconception: Anything that is not obviously acidic is neutral, and a neutral solution contains no ions.
items.why: Neutral is heard as 'nothing there', and pH 7 is associated with pure water. Only pH 7 is neutral. A neutral solution still contains ions — equal numbers of H⁺ and OH⁻.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How is the burette prepared before filling?
items.correct: Rinse it with the solution it will hold, then fill and remove the air bubble below the tap.
items.misconception: Rinsing with water is enough, because water is clean.
items.why: Rinsing is associated with cleaning, and water is the standard cleaning liquid. Water left in the burette dilutes the solution and changes the titre. Rinse with the solution being used.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How is concentration in mol/dm³ calculated from moles and volume?
items.correct: Concentration = moles ÷ volume in dm³.
items.misconception: Moles are multiplied by volume, the volume is divided by the concentration, or the two volumes in a titration are used the wrong way round.
items.why: The triangle is memorised without meaning, so any arrangement of the three quantities looks equally likely. Concentration is an amount per unit volume, so it must be a division. Use the volume of the solution whose concentration you want.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What does calling an acid weak tell you?
items.correct: That it is only partially ionised in solution.
items.misconception: That it is dilute, so there is not much of it.
items.why: Weak is heard as 'watered down', which is the everyday meaning. Weak describes the degree of ionisation. A weak acid can be concentrated, and a strong acid can be dilute.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: The pH falls by two units. Is that a tenfold change?
items.correct: No. It is a hundredfold change in hydrogen ion concentration.
items.misconception: Any fall in pH means a factor of ten.
items.why: The rule 'one unit is ten times' is remembered, but it is applied once however many units change. Apply the factor of 10 once for each unit: two units gives 10², three units gives 10³.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can a weak acid be concentrated?
items.correct: Yes. Weak and concentrated describe different things.
items.misconception: A weak acid must be dilute, and a concentrated acid must be strong.
items.why: The four words are learned as two opposite pairs and are then assumed to line up with each other. Concentration and strength vary independently: concentrated ethanoic acid is a concentrated weak acid.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which ion is common to all acids in aqueous solution?
items.correct: The hydrogen ion, H⁺.
items.misconception: Each acid produces the ion named in its own name, such as chloride from hydrochloric acid.
items.why: The negative ion is the one that appears in the salt, so it is the one students focus on. The negative ion differs from acid to acid; H⁺ is what makes all of them acids.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: The pH falls from 5 to 3. How many factors of ten is that?
items.correct: Two, giving a factor of 100.
items.misconception: Three, because the values 5, 4 and 3 have been counted.
items.why: Counting the numbers listed rather than the gaps between them is the same slip as counting fence posts instead of gaps. Subtract the pH values: 5 − 3 = 2 units, so the factor is 10² = 100.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Where does the metal ion in a salt come from?
items.correct: From the base, alkali or carbonate.
items.misconception: From the water formed in the reaction.
items.why: Both products appear at the same time, so the source of each part of the salt is not tracked. Water is a separate product, made from H⁺ and OH⁻. The metal ion was in the base, alkali or carbonate all along.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is any of the salt left in the residue on the filter paper?
items.correct: No. The salt is soluble, so all of it is in the filtrate.
items.misconception: The salt is shared between the residue and the filtrate.
items.why: Mixtures are imagined as being split roughly in half by any separation. Filtration separates by solubility, not by proportion. Only insoluble material stays on the paper.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How do crystals form from a salt solution?
items.correct: By removing water, so the solution becomes saturated.
items.misconception: By adding water until crystals appear.
items.why: Crystals are associated with liquids, so adding more liquid seems to help them form. Adding water makes the solution more dilute, so crystals are less likely. Evaporate water instead.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does an alkaline solution contain hydrogen molecules?
items.correct: No. It contains hydroxide ions, OH⁻.
items.misconception: The H in OH⁻ means hydrogen gas is present.
items.why: The symbol H appears in the formula, and hydrogen gas is the H species students meet most often. The hydrogen in the hydroxide ion is bonded to oxygen. Hydrogen gas is H₂ and is not present in the solution.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What is the burette used for in a titration?
items.correct: To add one solution gradually and measure the volume delivered.
items.misconception: To measure the fixed volume placed in the conical flask.
items.why: The burette is the most prominent piece of apparatus, so it is assumed to do the important measuring. The fixed volume is measured with a pipette. The burette measures the variable volume added to reach the end point.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why is universal indicator unsuitable for a titration?
items.correct: Because its colour changes gradually rather than at a single point.
items.misconception: Because the indicator reacts with the acid and is used up.
items.why: Anything added to a reaction mixture is assumed to be a reactant. Indicators are present in tiny amounts and are not consumed. The problem is the gradual colour change.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which titre should be used if the results differ?
items.correct: The mean of the concordant titres.
items.misconception: The largest titre, or any single reading chosen at will.
items.why: Picking one number avoids the work of deciding which results agree. Discard the rough titre, check which results agree within 0.10 cm³, and average those.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How many moles are in 20.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ acid?
items.correct: 0.00200 mol — volume in dm³ multiplied by concentration.
items.misconception: 0.0200 mol, the converted volume on its own.
items.why: The conversion step feels like the whole calculation, so the multiplication is forgotten. Converting the units is only the first step. Moles = concentration × volume in dm³.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How are the two volumes in a titration used?
items.correct: Each volume is used with its own solution: moles from one, concentration for the other.
items.misconception: The two volumes are subtracted, or averaged, to give a single number.
items.why: Two similar numbers in a question invite an arithmetic operation between them. The volumes belong to different solutions. Find moles from the known solution, then divide by the other solution's volume in dm³.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A sodium hydroxide solution is 0.0800 mol/dm³. What is its concentration in g/dm³? (Mᵣ of NaOH = 40)
items.correct: 3.2 g/dm³, found by multiplying by Mᵣ.
items.misconception: 0.08 g/dm³ — the same number with different units.
items.why: Changing units often means only relabelling, so the conversion factor is overlooked. Moles and grams are different quantities. Multiply the concentration in mol/dm³ by Mᵣ to get g/dm³.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
